title:
End-to-End Performance
Modelling and Analysis
speaker: Sun Jiangeng
script: Hello everyone. We are Sun Jiangeng, Qian Tu and Lu Zipeng. Our project follows product images from industrial cameras to an edge server for AI quality inspection. We ask how routing, wireless scheduling and server queues affect delivery time, and which upgrades can help when traffic increases.

title: Three tasks, one image journey
speaker: Sun Jiangeng
script: The project has three connected tasks. We use graph theory to describe the network and select a route. We then use Shannon's formula and a polling schedule to calculate wireless delay. Finally, we use queueing theory to analyse the edge server. Python simulations test these calculations and connect the stages into a complete image journey.

title: The numerical inputs are explicit assumptions
speaker: Sun Jiangeng
script: The brief gives no numerical parameters, so we clearly label ours as assumptions. We use four cameras, one-megabit images, twenty megahertz of bandwidth and a ten-decibel signal-to-noise ratio. The MEC, or multi-access edge computing server, processes fifty images per second on average. Our chosen mean-delay target is one hundred milliseconds. Lambda always means the total arrival rate across all four cameras, divided equally between them.

title: A graph describes the available paths
speaker: Sun Jiangeng
script: The graph contains cameras, small base stations and the MEC server. Directed links carry capacities and propagation delays. Base station A can reach the server directly, or relay through base station B. The direct link has lower capacity than the two relay links. In this single-cell example, wireless images leave at least fourteen point six five milliseconds apart, while each relay link needs only one millisecond to transmit an image. Therefore these backhaul links do not queue. The wireless rate is available only to the camera currently scheduled.

title: A faster route can have an extra hop
speaker: Sun Jiangeng
script: Dijkstra's algorithm minimises the sum of nonnegative link delays: image size divided by link capacity, plus propagation. The direct wired backhaul takes eleven milliseconds per image. The two-hop backhaul takes two point seven milliseconds. Including the common wireless payload gives a selected route weight of seventeen point one five milliseconds. That weight excludes the grant, polling wait and MEC processing, which we add separately. The relay saves eight point three milliseconds. Qian will now explain when a camera can transmit and how long its wireless stage takes.

title: Shannon gives an ideal scheduled rate
speaker: Qian Tu
script: Shannon's rate is bandwidth multiplied by the base-two logarithm of one plus the linear signal-to-noise ratio. Ten decibels converts to a linear value of ten. Our scheduled rate is sixty-nine point one nine megabits per second, so a one-megabit image needs fourteen point four five milliseconds. We assign all OFDMA resource blocks to one camera per visit, reusing them in time. This is a simplified scheduling case with an ideal radio rate.

title: Random arrival phase creates polling wait
speaker: Qian Tu
script: The base station visits cameras one to four in a fixed cycle. Each visit includes overhead and at most one image. Empty visits remain reserved. One cycle lasts fifty-eight point six one milliseconds. For an isolated image arriving at a random phase, the mean wait is half a cycle. Adding its grant and payload gives forty-three point nine six milliseconds. This reference assumes no older image at that camera. It is different from a simultaneous batch arriving at the cycle boundary.

title: Backlog increases the camera waiting time
speaker: Qian Tu
script: When older images are waiting, a new image may wait through several visits. For our reserved one-image rule, the mean polling wait is C divided by two times the quantity one minus r. Here r is the utilisation of one camera's reserved visits. At a total arrival rate of twenty-five images per second, the wait is forty-six point two five milliseconds. This wait excludes the image's own grant and payload.

title: Image-size variability changes transmission service
speaker: Qian Tu
script: The brief also asks about random image size. If size X is exponential with mean S and transmission rate R is constant, duration X divided by R is exponential too. With Poisson input and a continuously available transmitter, that supports M/M/1. Fixed-size images instead give deterministic transmission service, supporting M/D/1 under those same conditions. Our cyclic polling and fixed overhead require separate treatment. MEC processing times are a different modelling assumption.

title: Simulation tests each stage and the whole chain
speaker: Qian Tu
script: We simulate both the isolated M/M/1 server and the actual polled chain. Each arrival-rate experiment uses thirty independent runs, with one hundred thousand measured images after a twenty-thousand-image warm-up. Confidence intervals use run averages because successive image delays are correlated. Ten deterministic tests pass, including the lecture example. We also check that the measured delay components add up. Lu will now explain the server bound and final results.

title: Little’s law gives the M/M/1 delay bound
speaker: Lu Zipeng
script: Here we analyse the required isolated server: Poisson arrivals, independent exponential processing and one server. State k counts waiting images plus the image being processed. Arrivals increase the state at rate lambda; departures reduce it at rate mu. Stability requires lambda below mu. Little's law connects the average number of images to their arrival rate and mean time. It gives T equal to one divided by the difference between mu and lambda. T includes waiting and processing. With mu equal to fifty and a one-hundred-millisecond limit, the maximum arrival rate is forty images per second.

title: The isolated server follows the theoretical curve
speaker: Lu Zipeng
script: This plot compares simulated server time with M/M/1 theory. The largest relative difference in the mean is zero point six two percent. At forty images per second, theory gives one hundred milliseconds and simulation gives ninety-nine point three eight. Ten of eleven pointwise ninety-five-percent intervals cover theory. Universal coverage is not guaranteed. As load approaches processing capacity, waiting grows sharply, so spare capacity is important for low delay.

title: End-to-end delay includes the upstream stages
speaker: Lu Zipeng
script: The complete chain has additional waiting and transmission stages. At twenty-five images per second, mean total delay is ninety-eight point five two milliseconds. At thirty, it is one hundred twelve point four eight. Twenty-five is therefore the highest tested rate meeting the mean target; it is not an exact continuous threshold. Polling changes the server's arrival pattern, so we simulate that actual pattern instead of assuming it remains Poisson.

title: Radio and processing should be upgraded together
speaker: Lu Zipeng
script: At forty images per second, we compare four designs using the same traffic assumptions. A faster server alone and more bandwidth alone still miss the mean target. Combining forty megahertz with a server rate of seventy-five images per second reduces the mean to fifty-seven point three one milliseconds, about sixty-seven percent below baseline. The bandwidth comparison holds SNR fixed at ten decibels, so power and cost must also be considered. About nine point five percent of images still miss the deadline: a low mean is not a per-image guarantee.

title: Design for the whole image journey
speaker: Lu Zipeng
script: To conclude, link capacity matters as well as hop count. Polling and server queues both affect delay. A server-only bound cannot guarantee end-to-end performance, and mean delay must be distinguished from deadline reliability. Thank you. We welcome your questions.
